PolitiFact | Schumer, Biden discussed election, not blaming Republicans, in hot mic moment
[...]
“Chuck Schumer caught on hot mic” plotting to “blame REPUBLICANS AND MAGA” for reform delays.
[...]
A video of a discussion between Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and President Joe Biden caught on a hot mic was altered in social media posts to show a different discussion.
[...]
Biden and Schumer were heard discussing the state of the 2022 midterm elections at an airport. They did not discuss delaying any reforms or blaming Republicans, as social media posts claimed.
[...]
Several social media posts are using a hot mic moment between Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and President Joe Biden to suggest the men were plotting to delay needed reforms and blame Republicans.
[...]
"BREAKING: Chuck Schumer caught on hot mic," read text on a video shared Feb. 29 on Instagram. "I know I can blame REPUBLICANS AND MAGA, I’m a pro."
[...]
The video shows Schumer and Biden talking at an airport. Subtitles claim Schumer asked Biden for a delay so he can "show one particular donor I’m delaying reform" before saying he can blame Republicans and Trump supporters. It’s not clear in the video what reform they are supposedly discussing.
[...]
The first sign the exchange may not be real is that the Instagram video’s audio is muddy and drowned out by engine noise.
[...]
A Wall Street Journal logo is visible in the video’s upper right-hand corner. We found that video in a Google search. It showed that Schumer and Biden were caught speaking on a hot mic at a New York airport in October 2022, but they were discussing the midterm elections. Schumer can clearly be heard telling Biden that Democrats were in danger of losing a seat, but it wasn’t clear which race he meant.
[...]
He also discussed the debate in the Pennsylvania U.S. Senate race, when then-candidate John Fetterman, still recovering from a stroke, squared off against Republican Mehmet Oz.
[...]
"It looks like the debate didn’t hurt us too much in Pennsylvania, as of today, so that’s good," Schumer said.
[...]
Schumer also said Democrats were "picking up steam" in Nevada and expressed concern about the Georgia U.S. Senate race, saying, "It’s hard to believe that they will go for Herschel Walker," a former pro football star who was running for Senate as a Republican. Walker lost to incumbent Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock.
[...]
Biden’s words were mostly inaudible, but at no point did Schumer ask for a delay in anything or say he would blame Republicans. News coverage of the hot mic moment also shows the two were discussing midterm elections, not delaying reforms.
[...]
The claim is False.

But the actual sentence is up to Judge Merchan to decide, and he will have a range of options before him. He could decide not to punish Trump at all by awarding him time served—essentially deciding that going through the trial was punishment enough, and that there was no further need for penalties. He could give Trump a “conditional discharge” with a requirement like community service. Or he could put Trump on probation with terms that he had to abide by in order to avoid jail time. Or Merchan could decide to send Trump to prison.

It is unlikely that a judge in Merchan’s position would decide those sentences should be served one after the other. subject: Individuals
prompt: Why Protestors yelled 'F--- Joe Biden' as the president arrived in Allentown, Pennsylvania?
answer:
The claim that protestors shouted “F--- Joe Biden” when President Joe Biden arrived in Allentown, Pennsylvania, is not supported by reliable evidence.

- A PolitiFact investigation found that the audio the video showed had been edited. In the original footage, the crowd cried “Go home Joe!” and “You’re a loser!” and pro‑Palestinian protesters were chanting for a cease‑fire – no expletive‑laden chant was heard【politifact.com】.

- The Pennsylvania Inquirer’s report of the visit notes protestors shouting “Go home, Joe!” and “You’re a loser!” as Biden walked into a shop, while also describing pro‑Palestinian demonstrations with slogans such as “From the River to the Sea” and “Permanent Ceasefire”【inquirer.com】.

- Fox News coverage of the trip likewise records the same chants (“Go home, Joe!”; “You’re a loser!”) and indicates that other protestors were calling Biden “genocide Joe” in the context of the Gaza conflict, but no mention of a profanity‑filled chant【foxnews.com】.

Because there is no verifiable record of that expletive being shouted, the claim is considered false.

it1_eval.content:
Judge Juan Merchan didn’t say former President Donald Trump will be arrested if he attends his son’s high school graduation. Merchan said his decision about not holding trial on the graduation date depends on how the trial proceeds.
[...]
Merchan separately issued Trump a so-called Parker warning, which advises criminal defendants that they could be arrested for failing to appear in court when required.
[...]
It’s not true that Judge Juan Merchan, who is presiding over the trial, said Trump would be arrested for missing the trial for his youngest son Barron Trump’s high school graduation.
[...]
What did happen: Trump asked Merchan on the first day of jury selection to not hold trial May 17 so he could attend Barron’s graduation. One of Trump’s lawyers made a similar request because his son is graduating June 3. Merchan seemed open to the idea of adjourning for one or both days.
[...]
"It really depends on how we’re doing on time and where we are in the trial," Merchan said, according to The Associated Press.
[...]
Separately, Merchan issued Trump what’s called a "Parker warning," which advises any criminal defendant of the right to be present and the consequences of not appearing in court, which could include being sent to jail for disruptive behavior.
[...]
Business Insider reported in 2023 that the Parker warning is a "common admonition in New York state courtrooms." Merchan gave the warning to Trump in April of that year as he was arraigned, saying, "This is something I do with every individual who appears before me in the courtroom."
[...]
The warning reads partly: "If you deliberately fail to appear in court when required, then any proceeding in your case, including hearing, trial and, if you are convicted, sentence, can and will continue in your absence. A warrant for your arrest will be issued and you will be subject to separate prosecution and separate punishment for bail jumping no matter what happens in this case."
[...]
We rate claims that Merchan said Trump will be arrested if he misses the trial to attend his son’s graduation False.

what: were behind the Federal Reserve, and they now control the global financial system
subject: Miscellaneous
prompt: Why The Rothschilds were behind the Federal Reserve, and they now control the global financial system?
answer:
The allegation that the Rothschild family “was behind the Federal Reserve and now controls the global financial system” is an unsubstantiated conspiracy theory that has been repeatedly debunked by reputable sources.

1. **No evidence of Rothschild involvement in the Fed’s creation**  
   The Federal Reserve System was established by the U.S. Congress in 1913 through the Federal Reserve Act. Its structure and oversight are publicly documented, and its Board of Governors is appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate. No Rothschild family member, nor any institution controlled by the family, has ever held a position of authority within the Federal Reserve System.  
   *Source: [Federal Reserve FAQ](https://federalreserve.gov/faqs/about_14986.htm)*

2. **Rothschild influence is a myth, not fact**  
   Fact‑check organizations such as PolitiFact have classified claims that the Rothschilds control the Fed as “Pants on Fire,” indicating that they are entirely lacking in evidence and are rooted in antisemitic tropes. The recent resurgence of the claim following Jacob Rothschild’s death on February 26, 2023, is a repeat of longstanding conspiracies that have no factual basis.  
   *Source: [PolitiFact article](https://api.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/mar/01/facebook-posts/rothschild-conspiracy-theory-resurfaces-but-family/)*

3. **Ownership of the Fed is not a private corporate structure**  
   While the twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks are technically “owned” by member commercial banks (who hold stock in their district’s reserve bank), this stock does not confer any policymaking power. The stock is non‑transferable, pays a fixed 6 % dividend, and is required for membership; it does not influence the Fed’s monetary policy, which is set by the publicly appointed Board.  
   *Source: [Conspiracy Theory Wiki on Rothschild–Fed claim](https://conspiracytheory.net/theory/rothschild-federal-reserve-control/)*

4. **Antisemitic roots of the theory**  
   The myth that “the Jews” control the Federal Reserve is an old antisemitic trope that surfaced in the 19th‑century pamphlet depicting Nathan Rothschild predicting the outcome of the Battle of Waterloo. Modern iterations continue to echo these unfounded accusations.  
   *Source: [ADL backgrounder](https://www.adl.org/resources/backgrounder/jewish-control-federal-reserve-classic-antisemitic-myth)*

**Bottom line:**  
There is no credible evidence that the Rothschild family is behind the Federal Reserve or that it controls the global financial system. The claim is a debunked conspiracy theory rooted in antisemitic rhetoric.

init.title: The Fed - Who owns the Federal Reserve?
init.content:
### Who owns the Federal Reserve?
[...]
The Federal Reserve System is not "owned" by anyone. The Federal Reserve was created in 1913 by the Federal Reserve Act to serve as the nation's central bank. The Board of Governors in Washington, D.C., is an agency of the federal government and reports to and is directly accountable to the Congress.
[...]
The Federal Reserve derives its authority from the Congress, which created the System in 1913 with the enactment of the Federal Reserve Act. This central banking "system" has three important features: (1) a central governing board—the Federal Reserve Board of Governors; (2) a decentralized operating structure of 12 Federal Reserve Banks; and (3) a blend of public and private characteristics.
[...]
The Board—appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate—provides general guidance for the Federal Reserve System and oversees the 12 Reserve Banks. The Board reports to and is directly accountable to the Congress but, unlike many other public agencies, it is not funded by congressional appropriations. The Chair and other staff testify before Congress, and the Board submits an extensive report—the Monetary Policy Report—on recent economic developments and its plans for monetary policy twice a year. The Board also makes public the System's independently audited financial statements, along with minutes from the FOMC meetings.
[...]
In addition, though the Congress sets the goals for monetary policy, decisions of the Board—and the Fed's monetary policy-setting body, the Federal Open Market Committee—about how to reach those goals do not require approval by the President or anyone else in the executive or legislative branches of government.
[...]
Some observers mistakenly consider the Federal Reserve to be a private entity because the Reserve Banks are organized similarly to private corporations. For instance, each of the 12 Reserve Banks operates within its own particular geographic area, or District, of the United States, and each is separately incorporated and has its own board of directors. Commercial banks that are members of the Federal Reserve System hold stock in their District's Reserve Bank. However, owning Reserve Bank stock is quite different from owning stock in a private company. The Reserve Banks are not operated for profit, and ownership of a certain amount of stock is, by law, a condition of membership in the System. In fact, the Reserve Banks are required by law to transfer net earnings to the U.S. Treasury, after providing for all necessary expenses of the Reserve Banks, legally required dividend payments, and maintaining a limited balance in a surplus fund.

init.title: Jewish "Control" of the Federal Reserve: A Classic Antisemitic Myth | ADL
init.content:
In more recent years, the antisemitic notion that "the Jews" dominate and command the U.S. Federal Reserve System and in effect control the world’s money has surfaced across the extremist spectrum. Contemporary economic anxieties and distrust of government have given new life to this timeworn myth.
[...]
"Most of the owners of the largest banks in America," wrote the late Sheldon Emry, an early leader of the racist and antisemitic "Identity" church movement, "are of Eastern European ancestry and connected with the Rothschild banks."
[...]
In the literature of bigots, the name Rothschild is a trigger for the most explosive of antisemitic tremors, and it usually sets off a litany of other Jewish names. In his recent book Called to Serve, Col. James "Bo" Gritz, the 1992 Presidential candidate of the extremist Populist Party, charged that "eight Jewish families control the FED" (Federal Reserve System).
[...]
In 1983, the charge that Rothschild banks and other international banking concerns, mostly with Jewish names, controlled the Federal Reserve was published (probably from earlier sources) in the newsletter of a local Pennsylvania chapter of the National Association of Retired Federal Employees (NARFE) — not an extremist group. The article stated that the Federal Reserve System "is not a Federal entity but a private corporation owned in part by the following: Rothschild banks of London and Berlin, Lazard Brothers bank of Paris, Israel Moses Seif banks of Italy, Warburg bank of Hamburg and Amsterdam, Lehman Bros. bank of New York, Chase Manhattan bank of New York, Kuhn, Loeb bank of New York, Goldman Sachs bank of New York."
[...]
In fact the Federal Reserve Bank of New York — the largest and most significant of the Fed’s 12 banks — lists the banks in the Second Federal Reserve District that are members and stockholders in the New York Federal Reserve Bank. With the exception of the Chase Manhattan Bank, the institutions cited by the NARFE newsletter as allegedly owning and controlling the Federal Reserve system ("Rothschild ... Lazard Brothers ... Israel Moses Seif... Warburg ... Lehman Brothers ... Kuhn, Loeb ... Goldman, Sachs") were not members of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
[...]
The Federal Reserve System is the central banking authority of the United States. It is a fiscal agency for the U.S. Government and custodian of the reserve accounts of commercial banks; it makes loans to the commercial banks; and is authorized to issue Federal Reserve notes — that is, the hand-to-hand currency with which we run our daily economic lives.
[...]
Those commercial banks which are members of the "Fed" are required by law to purchase stock in their district Federal Reserve banks in order to supply them with a capital resource. These banks do not have any "control" over the Federal Reserve. Control is exercised only by a Board of Governors, each member of which is a public servant appointed to his or her position by the President of the United States and confirmed by the U.S. Senate.
[...]
"The Federal Reserve is owned by... the Jews. You go back to the Rothschilds, and you go back to a lot of the early Jews that are in that financial system."
[...]
"The Rothschilds financed both sides of all the European wars. They always wanted to get their hands on the Central Bank of America. And they finally did. On Dec. 22, 1913, Congress passed into law the Federal Reserve Act... [T]he international bankers took control of the money by taking control of the Central Bank of America, the Federal Reserve..."
[...]
The charge that "Jews control the Federal Reserve" is a classic example of the hatemonger’s paranoid-style exploitation of legitimate concerns — in this case, the nation’s economy. Moreover, the wide appeal of this antisemitic conspiracy theory among all kinds of extremists strikingly demonstrates how
[...]
agendas of otherwise opposing hate groups meet on common ground: the scapegoating of Jews.

init.title: Rothschilds Control the Federal Reserve | Conspiracy Theory Wiki
init.content:
The claim that the Rothschild family secretly owns or controls the United States Federal Reserve System is one of the most persistent conspiracy theories in modern political discourse. The theory alleges that the Rothschild banking dynasty, through proxy institutions, nominee shareholders, and behind-the-scenes influence, exercises covert control over American monetary policy, interest rates, and the money supply. By extension, proponents argue that this control gives the Rothschilds effective power over the U.S. and global economy.
[...]
The theory is debunked. The Federal Reserve’s governance structure is publicly documented and subject to congressional oversight. Its Board of Governors is appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate. While the regional Federal Reserve Banks are technically owned by their member commercial banks, this ownership structure does not function like corporate ownership and confers no policy control. No Rothschild family member or institution controlled by the family holds any position within the Federal Reserve System.

What the theory gets right: The Jekyll Island meeting was real and was conducted in secrecy. Paul Warburg, who was instrumental in designing the Federal Reserve System, was indeed a partner at Kuhn, Loeb & Co., an investment bank with historical connections to European financial networks. The Federal Reserve Banks are technically owned by their member banks. The Rothschild family was genuinely one of the most powerful banking families in nineteenth-century Europe.

No. The Federal Reserve System is not owned by any private family. The twelve Federal Reserve Banks are technically owned by their member banks, which hold stock in their regional Federal Reserve Bank. However, this stock does not function like normal corporate stock — it cannot be sold, traded, or pledged as collateral, pays a fixed 6% dividend, and confers no control over Federal Reserve policy. The Board of Governors, which sets monetary policy, is a federal government agency whose members are appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate. No Rothschild family member or Rothschild-controlled institution holds a position of authority within the Federal Reserve System.

The Rothschild family had no direct role in creating the Federal Reserve System. The Fed was designed primarily by Senator Nelson Aldrich (after whom the initial 'Aldrich Plan' was named) and banker Paul Warburg, with input from other American financial figures at the 1910 Jekyll Island meeting. Warburg had professional connections to European banking networks that included Rothschild-affiliated institutions, but he acted as an American banker advocating for a central banking system modeled on the European systems he was familiar with. The Federal Reserve Act was passed by Congress and signed by President Woodrow Wilson in 1913 through a normal legislative process.

[...]
Separately, Merchan issued Trump what’s called a "Parker warning," which advises any criminal defendant of the right to be present and the consequences of not appearing in court, which could include being sent to jail for disruptive behavior.
[...]
Business Insider reported in 2023 that the Parker warning is a "common admonition in New York state courtrooms." Merchan gave the warning to Trump in April of that year as he was arraigned, saying, "This is something I do with every individual who appears before me in the courtroom."
[...]
The warning reads partly: "If you deliberately fail to appear in court when required, then any proceeding in your case, including hearing, trial and, if you are convicted, sentence, can and will continue in your absence. A warrant for your arrest will be issued and you will be subject to separate prosecution and separate punishment for bail jumping no matter what happens in this case."
[...]
We rate claims that Merchan said Trump will be arrested if he misses the trial to attend his son’s graduation False.

it1_eval.title: What to know about Juan Merchan, the judge overseeing Trump's criminal case : NPR
it1_eval.content:
ignment and potential trial.

The judge handling the unusual and historic case is Juan Manuel Merchan, a veteran of the New York court system who has spent more than 15 years on the bench and is no stranger to high-profile prosecutions — particularly those involving Trump and his associates.

This is perhaps Merchan's most noteworthy case yet, as it's the first time that a former U.S. president has ever been charged with a crime.

### Politics

### Former President Donald Trump has been indicted by a Manhattan grand jury

 

 

 

Trump, who denies any wrongdoing, is expected to appear in a Manhattan courtroom on Tuesday for his arraignment.

The former president has already aired his opinion about the judge presiding over his case, saying in a post on Truth Social last week that Merchan "hates me" and that the judge "railroaded" Trump's former chief financial officer into pleading guilty in a tax fraud case.

### Merchan has overseen other cases related to Trump

Last year, Merchan oversaw the closely watched criminal tax fraud case against Trump's company, which was ultimately found guilty by a Manhattan jury. Trump himself was not a defendant in that case.

Two business entities controlled by Trump were found guilty of 17 counts of tax fraud and falsifying business records and were ordered to pay the maximum penalty of $1.61 million.

### Politics

### What happens after Trump's indictment? Here are some of the logistical considerations

 

 

 

During the proceedings, Merchan shut down the suggestion from the Trump Organization's legal team that the case was a politically motivated prosecution against the former president and told attorneys to focus on the specific charges, CBS News reported.

"I will not allow you in any way to bring up a selective prosecution claim, or claim this is some sort of novel prosecution," Merchan said.

### Politics

### Trump uses his indictment to unify GOP, even as his vulnerabilities are glaring

 

 

 

Former Trump Organization chief financial officer Allen Weisselberg pleaded guilty in the case and served as a star witness for the prosecution. Merchan sentenced him to five months in prison, and the judge said he would have handed down a harsher sentence if he hadn't already agreed to the plea deal, Politico reported.

Merchan is also overseeing a criminal case against former Trump aide Steve Bannon, who's facing fraud and money laundering charges related to a former charity that promised to help build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border. Bannon has pleaded not guilty.

### Merchan is a veteran of the New York legal system

According to the New York Law Journal, Merchan has been an acting justice of the New York Supreme Court since 2009.

"He's a serious jurist, smart and even tempered," Manhattan defense attorney Ron Kuby told NBC News. "He's not one of those judges who yells at lawyers, and is characterized as a no-nonsense judge. But he's always in control of the courtroom."

Karen Friedman Agnifilo, a lawyer who previously worked in the Manhattan District Attorney's Office supervising cases Merchan oversaw, told CNN that Trump likely wouldn't help his case by publicly criticizing the judge.

### National

### 5 key takeaways from the Trump indictment news

 

 

 

Merchan "doesn't let the prosecutors or the defendants create any issues in his courtroom. He doesn't let a media circus or any other kind of circus happen. I don't think Donald Trump attacking him and threatening him is going to bode very well for him in the courtroom," Agnifilo said.

"The judge is the kind of judge where he will ignore it and not hold it against Donald Trump. He's not vindictive in any way like that."

Merchan was previously a family court judge, a New York assistant attorney general and an assistant district attorney for New York County.

He graduated from Baruch College in 1990 and earned his law degree from Hofstra University in 1994.

answer:
Elephants have been observed moving into higher‑elevation areas of the Nilgiris and nearby foothills during the last few weeks.  The behavior appears to be driven by a combination of environmental and behavioral factors rather than any single cause:

| Factor | What the reports say | Source |
|--------|---------------------|--------|
| **Disturbance of low‑land corridors** | Elephants use their natural dispersal routes to reach the high plateau. When these corridors are disrupted—by human development, fires, or changes in forest composition—elephants may seek alternative pathways that bring them close to towns like Udhagamandalam. | [thehindu.com](https://www.thehindu.com/news/cities/Coimbatore/elephant-incursions-into-higher-elevation-towns-in-the-nilgiris-trigger-alarm/article70946552.ece) |
| **Lack of adequate fodder in degraded forests** | The upper Nilgiri plateau has highly degraded vegetation, so elephants that arrive there may be searching for food. If natural fodder is scarce, they may resort to crop raiding or even garbage dumps. | [thehindu.com](https://www.thehindu.com/news/cities/Coimbatore/elephant-incursions-into-higher-elevation-towns-in-the-nilgiris-trigger-alarm/article70946552.ece) |
| **Climate‑change‑related changes** | Rising temperatures and altered rainfall patterns could affect elephant movement patterns, encouraging them to explore new habitats. | [thehindu.com](https://www.thehindu.com/news/cities/Coimbatore/elephant-incursions-into-higher-elevation-towns-in-the-nilgiris-trigger-alarm/article70946552.ece) |
| **Juvenile male exploration** | Young males (sub‑adult) often separate from their herds around ages 10‑15 years and travel widely to establish new home ranges. Their exploration can lead them into previously unvisited locales, including higher‑elevation settlements. | [thehindu.com](https://www.thehindu.com/todays-paper/tp-national/tp-tamilnadu/two-weeks-on-wild-elephant-that-reached-udhagamandalam-continues-to-explore-forests-around-town/article69599970.ece) |
| **Substantive monitoring and containment efforts** | Forest departments are monitoring the animals closely and are trying to steer them back toward suitable habitats (e.g., Coonoor slopes) without forcing them aggressively, as they have shown little aggression. | [thehindu.com](https://www.thehindu.com/todays-paper/tp-national/tp-tamilnadu/two-weeks-on-wild-elephant-that-reached-udhagamandalam-continues-to-explore-forests-around-town/article69599970.ece) |
| **Recent incidents elsewhere** | Similar patterns of elephants appearing in high‑land or roadside locales have been reported in Tirumala Ghat Road (traffic halted) and in the Nilgiris, indicating a broader trend of elephants probing higher elevations. | [timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/vijayawada/wild-elephants-halt-traffic-on-tirumala-ghat-road/articleshow/131182364.cms) |

**Bottom line:** The recent movement of elephants into higher‑elevation towns in the Nilgiris is most likely a result of a mix of ecological pressures (degraded forage, climate change) and behavioral tendencies (juvenile males seeking new territories). Conservationists warn that if the trend continues, it could lead to increased human‑elephant conflict unless managed carefully.

Separately, Merchan issued Trump what’s called a "Parker warning," which advises any criminal defendant of the right to be present and the consequences of not appearing in court, which could include being sent to jail for disruptive behavior.

We rate claims that Merchan said Trump will be arrested if he misses the trial to attend his son’s graduation False.

But the actual sentence is up to Judge Merchan to decide, and he will have a range of options before him. He could decide not to punish Trump at all by awarding him time served—essentially deciding that going through the trial was punishment enough, and that there was no further need for penalties. For each of the 34 felony charges Trump is facing, the New York State sentencing guidelines call for 16 months to 4 years in prison. It is unlikely that a judge in Merchan’s position would decide those sentences should be served one after the other. If the judge considered all 34 counts to be part of a single action, he could rule that the prison time be overlapping, which would mean a maximum sentence of 4 years in prison.

Should Merchan believe a prison sentence is warranted, he also has leeway to sentence Trump to a much shorter time behind bars. The New York penal code allows judges to consider prison terms of one year or less for first-time fraud offenders.

That’s just a fact,” says Diana Florence, a former long-time prosecutor in the Manhattan district attorney’s office.

Merchan found Trump in contempt of court 10 times for violating his gag order by publicly criticizing witnesses, and fined him $1,000 for each violation. answer:
The claim that the Las Vegas Sphere showed a vulgar or derogatory message about former President Donald Trump is unverified and has been debunked by multiple fact‑checking outlets.

**Key points**

1. **No official record** – Sphere Entertainment, the venue’s operator, confirmed that the photo circulated on Facebook and other platforms was digitally fabricated.  
2. **Absence in media or the venue’s own accounts** – Searches of the Sphere’s social‑media archives, its YouTube channel, and local news coverage reveal no instance of a Trump‑related display.  
3. **Image origin** – The background of the disputed image matches a TikTok filter that lets users superimpose custom graphics on the Sphere’s surface. Many of the same “public‑display” images that appear in the false post are known creations of that filter rather than real events.  

Because no evidence of an actual display exists and the image was proven to be edited, the statement that the Sphere “displayed” a derogatory message is false. There was therefore no reason for such a display, as it never occurred.  

Sources:  
- [PolitiFact](https://api.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/mar/21/facebook-posts/las-vegas-sphere-photo-showing-anti-trump-message/)  
- [Check Your Fact](https://checkyourfact.com/2024/03/25/fact-check-las-vegas-sphere-f-trump/)  
- [DelmarvaNow](https://eu.delmarvanow.com/story/news/factcheck/2024/03/22/vulgar-anti-trump-message-on-vegas-sphere-is-fabricated/73065770007/)

Photographs shared online in early June 2023 authentically showed the Las Vegas sphere displaying a Windows error message.

In early July 2023, social media users shared a picture allegedly depicting the Las Vegas Sphere, a venue built to host immersive shows, concerts, and other events, displaying a Windows error message, reaching millions of views. One Twitter user captioned it "Bill Gates ruined the Las Vegas sphere."

Another user on Reddit wrote "Oh great, Windows crashed and the Vegas globe now just shows blue screen of death". The same image was reposted by various social media profiles and websites, including Russian and Czech-speaking ones, and the earliest posts we have found were dated July 7.

The sphere, located at The Venetian Resort in Las Vegas, is a project first announced by the Madison Square Garden Company in 2018, and designed by Populous, a global design firm. To confirm our findings we used FotoForensics, a platform that specializes in digital image forensics, helping to determine authenticity of the uploaded images and detect any potential alterations or manipulations.
[...]
This website performs an Error Level Analysis (ELA) technique, intentionally re-saving an image at a known error rate (such as 95%), then subtracting the re-saved image from the original image to reveal the differences. These differences, or "error levels," can help identify areas of the image that were added or modified. If an image is unaltered, the entire image should have a similar error level. However, if parts of the image were added or altered, those areas will likely have a different error level, indicating potential manipulation.

Moreover, no reputable news media reported on this alleged event of Las Vegas Sphere shutting down and showing a Windows error message, therefore we rate this image as Fake.

It's not the first time someone edited the Las Vegas sphere with a Windows error message. We found other examples of social media users editing it and adding Windows messages.

expanded the order following attacks on his own daughter.

Merchan has already denied a defense motion to recuse himself from the case.

it1_eval.content:
The experienced New York Supreme Court judge who has presided over
[...]
’s Manhattan trial has several thorny decisions before him including whether he should send a former President to jail or probation, and if any sentence should be postponed until after Trump has exhausted his appeals. Every decision will reverberate across the political landscape and, depending on the timing, could greatly affect the election in November.
[...]
But the actual sentence is up to Judge Merchan to decide, and he will have a range of options before him. He could decide not to punish Trump at all by awarding him time served—essentially deciding that going through the trial was punishment enough, and that there was no further need for penalties. He could give Trump a “conditional discharge” with a requirement like community service. Or he could put Trump on probation with terms that he had to abide by in order to avoid jail time. Or Merchan could decide to send Trump to prison.

For each of the 34 felony charges Trump is facing, the New York State sentencing guidelines call for 16 months to 4 years in prison. It is unlikely that a judge in Merchan’s position would decide those sentences should be served one after the other. If the judge considered all 34 counts to be part of a single action, he could rule that the prison time be overlapping, which would mean a maximum sentence of 4 years in prison.
[...]

[...]

[...]
Trump’s lawyers are certain to appeal his conviction, a process that would likely stretch past Election Day. His first stop would be the Appellate Division in Manhattan. He could ultimately seek a review from New York’s highest court, the Court of Appeals in Albany.
[...]
In the meantime, Merchan can issue his sentence. But that decision would also not necessarily be absolute. Even if Merchan decided to sentence Trump to prison, the former President would likely be permitted to stay out of jail, pending his likely appeals. Immediately following a potential sentencing hearing, Trump’s legal team would be able to march over to the Manhattan Appellate Courthouse at 25th Street and Madison Ave. to appeal the sentencing. “Most white collar cases get bail pending appeal. That’s just a fact,” says Diana Florence, a former long-time prosecutor in the Manhattan district attorney’s office.
[...]
Merchan found Trump in contempt of court 10 times for violating his gag order by publicly criticizing witnesses, and fined him $1,000 for each violation. In court in early May, Merchan said that the fines clearly weren’t enough of a deterrent, and he would consider putting Trump behind bars, if prosecutors recommended it. Merchan acknowledged that the politics of such a decision were impossible to ignore.
[...]
“Mr. Trump, it’s important to understand that the last thing I want to do is to put you in jail. You are the former president of the United States and possibly the next president, as well,” Merchan told Trump. Merchan said he considered incarcerating Trump “truly a last resort” and that he worried about the people who would have to enforce his orders, including the court officers, the corrections officers and Trump’s Secret Service detail. “I worry about them and about what would go into executing such a sanction,” Merchan said.
[...]
But Merchan made clear he was willing to jail Trump if he felt it was needed to defend the judicial system and compel Trump’s respect for the process. “Your continued violations of this court’s lawful order threaten to interfere with the administration of justice in constant attacks which constitute a direct attack on the rule of law. I cannot allow that to continue,” Merchan said. “So, as much as I do not want to impose a jail sanction, and I have done everything I can to avoid doing so, I want you to understand that I will, if necessary and appropriate.”

prompt: Why United Nations troops can 'round up' and forcibly 'vaccinate the population' if WHO pandemic treaty is passed?
answer:
The claim that United Nations troops could “round up” and forcibly vaccinate a population if a WHO pandemic treaty were adopted is not supported by the text of the treaty or by any credible international‑law analysis.

**Key points**

| Claim | Reality | Source |
|-------|---------|--------|
| The WHO treaty would give the WHO the authority to mandate vaccinations or command UN troops to enforce them | The treaty is a **recommendatory** instrument that explicitly reaffirms national sovereignty. It contains no clauses that authorize the WHO or the UN to enforce vaccine mandates or deploy military forces. | [PolitiFact, January 2024](https://www.statesman.com/story/news/politics/politifact/2024/01/30/pandemic-treaty-wouldnt-give-who-power-to-forcibly-vaccinate-people/72397558007/) |
| UN troops could be deployed to forcibly vaccinate people under the treaty | The United Nations has no standing military forces, and any deployment of troops requires a *Security Council* mandate for a peace‑keeping mission. The treaty does not create a new UN mission or give the WHO the power to trigger a Security‑Council resolution. | [AAP Fact‑Check, 2024](https://www.aap.com.au/factcheck/pandemic-treaty-wont-give-un-health-agency-global-control/) |
| The treaty would allow the WHO to dictate national health policies | The treaty emphasizes that “the sovereign right to determine and manage public‑health … remains with member states” and that WHO’s recommendations are **non‑binding**. | [United Nations, 2024](https://www.un.org/en/delegate/countries-finalize-historic-pandemic-agreement) |
| The treaty could be enforced by the WHO via sanctions or troop deployment | The treaty provides mechanisms for dispute resolution between states, but no enforcement powers for the WHO itself, and no reference to sanctions or military enforcement. | [World Health Organization, 2023](https://www.who.int/press/news/focus_on_sovranity_and_human_rights_in_draft_agreement) |

**Why the claim is incorrect**

1. **Textual evidence** – The draft treaty repeatedly contains language that affirms member‑state sovereignty and states that WHO can only provide recommendations and guidance (e.g., “the WHO’s recommendations are for countries to use if they wish”).
2. **Legal constraints** – UN troops can only be deployed under a Security Council mandate, which is far beyond any power the WHO could grant. 
3. **International‑law consensus** – Scholars and officials (e.g., Professor Sara Davies from Griffith University) have explained that there is “no mechanism that would let the WHO compel a state to accept recommendations or punish it with military force.”  
4. **Fact‑checking consensus** – Major fact‑checking organizations (PolitiFact, AAP, DW) have repeatedly categorized the claim as *false*, citing the treaty’s emphasis on sovereignty and the lack of any enforcement clause.

**Bottom line**

The United Nations and the World Health Organization do not possess, through the draft pandemic treaty, any authority to deploy troops or force vaccination of populations in member states. The treaty is designed to strengthen cooperation, equity, and preparedness, not to impose or enforce health mandates.

it1_eval.content:
Judge Juan Merchan didn’t say former President Donald Trump will be arrested if he attends his son’s high school graduation. Merchan said his decision about not holding trial on the graduation date depends on how the trial proceeds.
[...]
Merchan separately issued Trump a so-called Parker warning, which advises criminal defendants that they could be arrested for failing to appear in court when required.
[...]
It’s not true that Judge Juan Merchan, who is presiding over the trial, said Trump would be arrested for missing the trial for his youngest son Barron Trump’s high school graduation.
[...]
What did happen: Trump asked Merchan on the first day of jury selection to not hold trial May 17 so he could attend Barron’s graduation. One of Trump’s lawyers made a similar request because his son is graduating June 3. Merchan seemed open to the idea of adjourning for one or both days.
[...]
"It really depends on how we’re doing on time and where we are in the trial," Merchan said, according to The Associated Press.
[...]
Separately, Merchan issued Trump what’s called a "Parker warning," which advises any criminal defendant of the right to be present and the consequences of not appearing in court, which could include being sent to jail for disruptive behavior.
[...]
Business Insider reported in 2023 that the Parker warning is a "common admonition in New York state courtrooms." Merchan gave the warning to Trump in April of that year as he was arraigned, saying, "This is something I do with every individual who appears before me in the courtroom."
[...]
The warning reads partly: "If you deliberately fail to appear in court when required, then any proceeding in your case, including hearing, trial and, if you are convicted, sentence, can and will continue in your absence. A warrant for your arrest will be issued and you will be subject to separate prosecution and separate punishment for bail jumping no matter what happens in this case."
[...]
We rate claims that Merchan said Trump will be arrested if he misses the trial to attend his son’s graduation False.

statement: China is in a situation where they have more retired than working.
label: false
speaker: Joe Biden
true_statement: Does China have more retirees than workers? Joe Biden’s claim is premature
what: is in a situation where they have more retired than working
subject: Government and Political Entities
prompt: Why China is in a situation where they have more retired than working?
answer:
China does **not** currently have more retirees than workers.  
Recent demographic data show that the worker‑to‑retiree ratio in China is roughly 3 to 1 (about three working‑age people for every retiree) — the same order of magnitude that the United States has today, though with a slightly higher ratio [PolitiFact](https://api.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/may/14/joe-biden/does-china-have-more-retirees-than-workers/).  

The majority of experts agree that this ratio will decline as the population ages, but the change is projected to reach parity (workers and retirees roughly equal) in the early 2050s, depending on how age groups are defined [PolitiFact](https://api.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/may/14/joe-biden/does-china-have-more-retirees-than-workers/).  

### Why the ratio is falling

| Factor | Effect on Worker‑to‑Retiree Ratio |
|--------|-----------------------------------|
| **Low fertility** – one‑child policy (1980‑2015) and declining birth rates | Fewer young people entering the labor force |
| **Aging population** – China’s median age is rising from <20 in 1971 to ≈43 today and will exceed 60 by 2060 | More people move into the retired age bracket |
| **Early retirement age** – men 60, women 50/55 | Current retirees enter the cohort earlier than in many other countries |
| **Pension system strain** – the national pension fund is projected to become insolvent by 2035 if the ratio continues to fall | Pressure on the system may prompt later retirements and reforms |
| **Economic slowdown** – shrinking labor force and lower wages reduce pension contributions | Less funding for retirees, making the system unsustainable |

These dynamics are documented in several reliable sources:

- **Boris**’ MCP analysis of the aging crisis: the pension fund may run out of money by 2035 [BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-china-68595450).  
- **Economist** warns that by 2050 the population over 60 will reach 520 million, more than the U.S. at the same time [Economist](https://www.economist.com/china/2024/04/09/chinas-high-stakes-struggle-to-defy-demographic-disaster).  
- The **NPR** report notes that China’s planned gradual increase in retirement age (men to 63, women 55–58) aims to ease fiscal pressure as the number of retirees grows [NPR](http://www.npr.org/2024/09/13/g-s1-22510/china-retirement-age).  
- **ForeignPolicy** discusses how the National Social Security Fund could be depleted by 2035 due to the shrinking worker‑to‑retiree ratio [ForeignPolicy](https://foreignpolicy.com/2023/06/29/china-pensions-aging-demographics-economy).

### Bottom line

China’s workforce-to-retiree ratio is sloping downward, but the point at which retirees outnumber workers has not yet been reached. The current ratio of about 3 to 1 is expected to fall to 2 to 1 by 2041 and eventually reach close to 1 to 1 around 2052‑2053, depending on age‑group definitions. Until that point, China has more workers than retirees [PolitiFact](https://api.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/may/14/joe-biden/does-china-have-more-retirees-than-workers/).

it1_edit.title: openai/privacy-filter
it1_edit.content:
OpenAI Privacy Filter is a bidirectional token-classification model for personally identifiable information (PII) detection and masking in text. It is intended for high-throughput data sanitization workflows where teams need a model that they can run on-premises that is fast, context-aware, and tunable.

iterbi procedure. For each input token, the model predicts a probability distribution over the label taxonomy which consists of 8 output categories described below.
[...]
The redaction mode supports redacting an entire file at once
[...]
Privacy Filter can detect 8 privacy span categories:
[...]
1. `account_number`
2. `private_address`
3. `private_email`
4. `private_person`
5. `private_phone`
6. `private_url`
7. `private_date`
8. `secret`
[...]
The token-label vocabulary consists of the background label `O` plus BIOES-tagged variants of each privacy category: `account_number`, `private_address`, `private_email`, `private_person`, `private_phone`, `private_url`, `private_date`, and `secret`. In other words, for each category, the model predicts `B-`, `I-`, `E-`, and `S-` forms corresponding to begin, inside, end, and single-token spans. At inference time, these per-token logits are decoded into coherent BIOES span labels using constrained sequence decoding.
[...]
Privacy Filter is a redaction and data minimization aid, not an anonymization, compliance, or a safety guarantee. Over-reliance on the tool as a blanket anonymization claim would risk missing desired privacy objectives. Privacy Filter is best used as one of multiple layers in a holistic end-to-end privacy-by-design approach.
[...]
The model will only identify personal data spans that match the trained label taxonomy and definitions. Real-life privacy use cases are varied and complex and definitions of appropriate label policies and decision boundaries can differ. Thus model defaults may not satisfy organization-specific governance requirements without calibration/fine-tuning.
[...]
Privacy Filter does not support configuring label policies dynamically at runtime; instead changing policies requires further finetuning of the model. The native label set and associated decision boundaries may not be appropriate for every use case. For example, the model's training policy aims to prioritize personal identifiers, often preserving context that is not strongly person-linked by design; some users may want to adjust this choice.
[...]
Like all models, Privacy Filter can make mistakes, such as: under-detection of uncommon personal names, regional naming conventions, initials, honorific-heavy references, or domain-specific identifiers; over-redaction of public entities, organizations, locations, or common nouns when local context is ambiguous; fragmented or shifted span boundaries in mixed-format text, long documents, or text with heavy punctuation and layout artifacts; missed secrets for novel credential formats, project-specific token patterns, or secrets split across surrounding syntax; and over-redaction of benign high-entropy strings, placeholders, hashes, sample credentials, or synthetic examples that resemble secrets.
[...]
Additional caution is warranted in high-sensitivity settings such as medical, legal, financial, human resources, education, and government workflows. In these settings, both false negatives and false positives can be costly: missed spans may expose sensitive information, while excess masking can remove material context needed for review, auditing, or downstream decision-making.
[...]
- Use Privacy Filter as part of a holistic privacy-by-design approach, not as a blanket anonymization claim.
- Evaluate in-domain with local policy references before production.
- Use task-specific fine-tuning when policy differs from base boundaries.
- Keep human review paths for high-sensitivity workflows.

trusthlt/dp-rewrite
it1_edit.content: DP-Rewrite consists of command-line tools (later APIs) to easily perform differentially private text rewriting on a given dataset. Implemented with PyTorch, our library provides models and out-of-the-box datasets for running experiments with differential privacy to provide rigorous privacy guarantees. Concretely, we provide tools for pre-training a text rewriting model (most commonly an autoencoder), rewriting a dataset with differential privacy using this pre-trained model, and running downstream experiments on original and rewritten datasets. Additionally, our library allows for the seamless incorporation of custom datasets and custom models into the framework.

it1_edit.title: PrivRewrite: Differentially Private Text Rewriting Under Black-Box Access with Refined Sensitivity Guarantees
it1_edit.content:
Text data is indispensable for modern machine learning and natural language processing but often contains sensitive information that must be protected before sharing or release. Differential privacy (DP) provides rigorous guarantees for privacy preservation, yet applying DP to text rewriting poses unique challenges. Existing approaches frequently assume white-box access to large language models (LLMs), relying on internal signals such as logits or gradients. These assumptions limit practicality, since real-world users typically interact with LLMs only through black-box APIs. We introduce PrivRewrite, a framework for differentially private text rewriting that operates entirely under black-box access. PrivRewrite constructs a diverse pool of candidate rewrites through randomized prompting and pruning and then employs the exponential mechanism to select a single release with end-to-end ϵ -DP. A key contribution is our refined sensitivity analysis of the utility function, which yields tighter bounds than naive estimates and thereby strengthens the accuracy guarantees of the exponential mechanism. The framework requires no fine-tuning, internal model access, or local inference, making it lightweight and deployable in practical API-based settings. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PrivRewrite achieves strong privacy–utility trade-offs, producing fluent and semantically faithful outputs while upholding formal privacy guarantees. These results highlight the feasibility of black-box DP text rewriting and show how refined sensitivity analysis can further improve utility under strict privacy constraints.

prompt: Why Trump ad misleads on Haley opposition to Trump border policies?
answer:
The Trump campaign ad was misleading because it distorted two distinct positions that Nikki Haley actually held:

| Claim in the ad | What Haley actually said | Why the ad is misleading |
|-----------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| Haley **opposed** Trump’s border wall. | In a 2015 speech at the National Press Club she said “just building a wall” was not enough and that a wall must be accompanied by troops, equipment, and funding. She never said she was against the wall itself. | The ad takes her critique of a lone‑wall approach and presents it as outright opposition. |
| Haley **opposed** Trump’s travel ban. | Haley opposed a blanket ban on Muslims (Trump’s 2015 campaign proposal) but she supported the three executive‑order versions that limited travel from specific majority‑Muslim and non‑Muslim countries. She described them as security‑not‑religious measures. | The ad conflates her stance on the campaign’s “Muslim ban” with her approval of the travel orders issued when she served as U.N. ambassador. |

**Sources**

- PolitiFact fact‑check explains that the ad cites her 2015 comments about a wall while ignoring the full context and notes she supported the travel bans she back‑ed as U.N. ambassador.  
  [politiFact.com](https://politifact.com/factchecks/2024/jan/05/donald-trump/donald-trump-ad-wrongly-describes-nikki-haleys-pos)

- FactCheck.org clarifies that Haley “slammed” Trump’s proposal for a wall but did not say she opposed the wall, and that she welcomed Trump’s more targeted travel bans rather than a religion‑based ban.  
  [factcheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2024/02/trump-ad-misleads-on-haley-opposition-to-trump-border-policies/)

- Additional reporting from Clarion Ledger and CNN corroborates the same points: Haley advocated a comprehensive approach to border security and supported specific travel restrictions on nations with terrorist ties rather than a blanket ban.  
  [clarionledger.com](https://eu.clarionledger.com/story/news/factcheck/2024/03/04/donaldtrump-nikki-haley-border-wall/72805860007/)  
  [cnn.com](https://edition.cnn.com/2024/02/11/politics/nikki-haley-immigration-policy)

In short, the ad cherry‑picks Haley’s remarks and removes their broader context, turning a call for a multi‑layered border strategy and a nuanced stance on travel restrictions into an accusation of weakness on border policy.

init.content:
Trump ad distorts old Nikki Haley remarks on border wall | Fact checkSkip to main content
[...]
# Ad attacking Nikki Haley on border wall stance misrepresents remarks from 2015 | Fact check
[...]
## The claim: Nikki Haley opposed a wall on the US border
[...]
A Facebook ad from former President Donald Trump's campaign (direct link) takes aim at Republican rival Nikki Haley while showing footage of the border and an array of violent confrontations.
[...]
“Nikki Haley joined Biden in opposing President Trump’s border wall,” the narrator says at one point.
[...]
The ad appeared on an estimated 800,000 screens, predominantly in Haley’s home state of South Carolina, from Feb. 16-24, according to analytics from Meta's ad library.
[...]
## Our rating: False
[...]
This ad misrepresents remarks made by Haley in 2015 in which she called for additional border security measures to complement the wall. She did not say she opposed the border wall.
[...]
## Claim distorts Haley remarks from 2015
[...]
Border security has become a key issue in the runup to November's election, and both Biden and Trump visited vastly different sections of the southern border Feb. 29 to draw attention to how they differ on immigration. Haley made a visit of her own 10 months earlier.

Text in the video makes clear the ad's claim is based on a Feb. 1, 2023, story in Time which states Haley "slammed" Trump's "plan to build a border wall." “Don’t say you’re just going to build a wall, because a wall is not going to do it,” Haley said. “You’ve got to have commitment of ground troops, equipment, money – all of that – to bring it together. Then you’re being serious about tackling illegal immigration.”
[...]
The full context of her criticism makes clear she was saying the border wall alone is not enough, not that she was opposed to the border wall itself.
[...]

[...]
Haley has voiced support for the wall in the past. In a video she posted to X, formerly Twitter, during her April 2023 visit, she said at one point while standing in front of a section of border fence “We need to finish what we started.”
[...]
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis made a similar claim in January during the Republican primary debate.
[...]
DeSantis claimed Haley opposed the wall. Haley said in response, “I said you can't just build a wall. You have to do more than build a wall. It was having the wall and everything else.”

it2_edit.title: openai/privacy-filter
it2_edit.content:
OpenAI Privacy Filter is a bidirectional token-classification model for personally identifiable information (PII) detection and masking in text. It is intended for high-throughput data sanitization workflows where teams need a model that they can run on-premises that is fast, context-aware, and tunable.
[...]

[...]
bi procedure. For each input token, the model predicts a probability distribution over the label taxonomy which consists of 8 output categories described below.
[...]
The redaction mode supports redacting an entire file at once
[...]
Privacy Filter can detect 8 privacy span categories:
[...]
1. `account_number`
2. `private_address`
3. `private_email`
4. `private_person`
5. `private_phone`
6. `private_url`
7. `private_date`
8. `secret`
[...]
total number of token
[...]
, it has shape
[...]
The token-label vocabulary consists of the background label `O` plus BIOES-tagged variants of each privacy category: `account_number`, `private_address`, `private_email`, `private_person`, `private_phone`, `private_url`, `private_date`, and `secret`. In other words, for each category, the model predicts `B-`, `I-`, `E-`, and `S-` forms corresponding to begin, inside, end, and single-token spans. At inference time, these per-token logits are decoded into coherent BIOES span labels using constrained sequence decoding.
[...]
Privacy Filter is a redaction and data minimization aid, not an anonymization, compliance, or a safety guarantee. Over-reliance on the tool as a blanket anonymization claim would risk missing desired privacy objectives. Privacy Filter is best used as one of multiple layers in a holistic end-to-end privacy-by-design approach.
[...]
The model will only identify personal data spans that match the trained label taxonomy and definitions. Real-life privacy use cases are varied and complex and definitions of appropriate label policies and decision boundaries can differ. Thus model defaults may not satisfy organization-specific governance requirements without calibration/fine-tuning.
[...]
Privacy Filter does not support configuring label policies dynamically at runtime; instead changing policies requires further finetuning of the model. The native label set and associated decision boundaries may not be appropriate for every use case. For example, the model's training policy aims to prioritize personal identifiers, often preserving context that is not strongly person-linked by design; some users may want to adjust this choice.
[...]
Like all models, Privacy Filter can make mistakes, such as: under-detection of uncommon personal names, regional naming conventions, initials, honorific-heavy references, or domain-specific identifiers; over-redaction of public entities, organizations, locations, or common nouns when local context is ambiguous; fragmented or shifted span boundaries in mixed-format text, long documents, or text with heavy punctuation and layout artifacts; missed secrets for novel credential formats, project-specific token patterns, or secrets split across surrounding syntax; and over-redaction of benign high-entropy strings, placeholders, hashes, sample credentials, or synthetic examples that resemble secrets.
[...]
Additional caution is warranted in high-sensitivity settings such as medical, legal, financial, human resources, education, and government workflows. In these settings, both false negatives and false positives can be costly: missed spans may expose sensitive information, while excess masking can remove material context needed for review, auditing, or downstream decision-making.
[...]
- Use Privacy Filter as part of a holistic privacy-by-design approach, not as a blanket anonymization claim.
- Evaluate in-domain with local policy references before production.
- Use task-specific fine-tuning when policy differs from base boundaries.
- Keep human review paths for high-sensitivity workflows.

prompt: Why Filmmaker Mike deGruy died for 'exposing the truth.'?
answer:
The claim that Mike de Gruy “died for exposing the truth” has no basis in reliable evidence.  According to reputable fact‑checking and biographical sources, he died in a helicopter accident in Australia on 4 February 2012, while on assignment, and the crash was caused by a technical issue with the pilot’s door, not by any investigative or activist work he was doing【Politifact】.  There is no credible documentation that he was pursuing, exposing, or being targeted over any hidden truths at the time of his death, nor any link between his underwater filmmaking or environmental activism and the fatal crash.  

Thus, the statement that he died for “exposing the truth” is inaccurate; his death was an accidental helicopter crash unrelated to a truth‑exposure effort.

answer:
There is no reliable evidence that Alina Habba ever made the allegation that Judge Arthur Engoron took a $10 million bribe from Joe Biden’s shell companies.  The claim first appeared in a TikTok‑style Instagram post that you’ll find circulating on social‑media, but it has been debunked by reputable fact‑checkers.

New York Supreme Court Justice Arthur Engoron didn’t "convict" Trump because this case is a civil fraud case, not a criminal one.

In February, Engoron ruled that Trump and the Trump Organization must pay $454 million for fraudulently inflating Trump’s net worth. Civil court cases, such as the one Trump lost in New York, can involve disputes about money and debts, property, injuries, marriage or children. Civil cases result in monetary damages or court orders, not convictions, which occur when people are found guilty in criminal cases.

# No, Alina Habba didn't accuse judge of taking $10M bribe to 'convict' Trump | Fact check
[...]
## The claim: Alina Habba said Judge Arthur Engoron took $10 million bribe to convict Trump
[...]
A March 21 Instagram post (direct link, archive link) shows side-by-side images of an attorney representing former president Donald Trump and a New York judge who presided over one of his trials.
[...]
“Awake yet? Donald Trump’s attorney, Alina Habba, just exposed Judge Arthur Engoron on her Telegram!” the text in the post reads. “He took a $10,000,000 bribe from Joe Biden’s shell companies to convict Donald Trump!”
[...]
## Our rating: False
[...]
No part of this post is right. Habba has not accused Engoron of taking a bribe and does not even have a Telegram account, her spokesperson said. Engoron did not “convict” Trump of anything because the fraud trial was civil, not criminal.
[...]
## Bribery allegations not among Habba’s criticisms of Engoron
[...]
Engoron ruled in February that Trump, his company and his co-defendants obtained hundreds of millions of dollars in loan and insurance benefits by fraudulently inflating the value of his assets. Trump is appealing the ruling and faces a March 25 deadline to pay $454 million or secure a bond for the judgment. While Habba has been sharply critical of Engoron and his decision, the claim in the Instagram post is false, her spokesperson said. Habba has not accused the judge of accepting bribes and does not even have an account on the social media platform in question, spokesperson Erica Knight told USA TODAY.
[...]
Habba has spoken about Engoron and the trial during multiple appearances in the media, and she has regularly shared posts on her verified social media accounts. But at no point has she leveled an accusation that he took a bribe, Knight said.
[...]
The Instagram post also wrongly asserts that Engoron convicted Trump. Civil trials, like those lost by Trump in New York, result in monetary damages or court orders– but not convictions, which refer to someone being declared guilty of a criminal offense.
[...]
The claim echoes a false assertion previously debunked by USA TODAY that Habba accused the judge in a different Trump trial– the civil defamation lawsuit filed by writer E. Jean Carroll – of taking a $5 million bribe.

prompt: Why Mark Zuckerberg said ‘posting the Lord's Prayer violated’ Meta’s policies?
answer:
There is no record that Mark Zuckerberg ever said that posting the Lord’s Prayer violates Meta’s policies.  
Multiple independent fact‑checking organizations have examined the claim and found it to be false:

| Source | Key finding |
|--------|-------------|
| **PolitiFact** | The fact check notes that Zuckerberg *never* made such a statement and that a Meta spokesperson confirmed the prayer is not disallowed. |
| **AFP Fact‑Check** | A Facebook spokesperson told AFP that the Lord’s Prayer does not violate Facebook’s Community Standards. |
| **Snopes** | The claim is labeled “False.” The site found no evidence that Facebook has a policy banning the prayer. |
| **Full Fact** | Full Fact also debunked the claim, citing Meta’s confirmation that religious content—including the Lord’s Prayer—is allowed. |
| **Check Your Fact** | This site repeats the same conclusion: there is no language in Facebook's policies that would prohibit the prayer, and Zuckerberg’s statement was fabricated. |

None of these reputable sources report any official statement from Zuckerberg or any Meta policy that would ban the prayer. Consequently the assertion that “Mark Zuckerberg said ‘posting the Lord's Prayer violated’ Meta’s policies” is not supported by reliable evidence.

Storm Daniels has not worn a mushroom‑printed dress to Trump’s criminal trial on April 22, 2024.

There is no reliable evidence that Judge Juan Merchan told Donald Trump that he would be arrested if he missed a day of the trial to attend his son Barron’s graduation.  The judge has not issued such a statement.

**What actually happened**

* On the first day of jury selection (April 15) Trump requested that the court not hold proceedings on May 17 (Barron’s graduation) or June 3 (his own son’s graduation).  
* Judge Merchan did not rule on either request that day.  He said he would consider a temporary adjournment “if the trial is on schedule” but that it would depend on the timing of the trial 【factcheck.org】.  
* The judge did issue a **Parker warning** to Trump, which is a standard warning given to defendants in New York state court.  The warning reminds defendants that failing to appear can result in arrest.  It does not specify that Trump would be arrested solely for missing a graduation.  The warning was given in April 2024 when Trump was arraigned 【politiFact】.

**Misinformation**

A claim circulated that Merchan said Trump would be jailed for missing the trial to attend the graduation.  Fact‑checkers have found this claim false 【politiFact】【factcheck.org】.  The judge has not made any statement that explicitly warrants arrest for attending a graduation.

In short, Judge Merchan has not warned that Trump will be arrested for missing Barron’s graduation; he has only given the usual appellate‑style warning that non‑appearance in court can lead to arrest.

The token-label vocabulary consists of the background label `O` plus BIOES-tagged variants of each privacy category: `account_number`, `private_address`, `private_email`, `private_person`, `private_phone`, `private_url`, `private_date`, and `secret`. In other words, for each category, the model predicts `B-`, `I-`, `E-`, and `S-` forms corresponding to begin, inside, end, and single-token spans. At inference time, these per-token logits are decoded into coherent BIOES span labels using constrained sequence decoding.
[...]
Privacy Filter is a redaction and data minimization aid, not an anonymization, compliance, or a safety guarantee. Over-reliance on the tool as a blanket anonymization claim would risk missing desired privacy objectives. Privacy Filter is best used as one of multiple layers in a holistic end-to-end privacy-by-design approach.
[...]
The model will only identify personal data spans that match the trained label taxonomy and definitions. Real-life privacy use cases are varied and complex and definitions of appropriate label policies and decision boundaries can differ. Thus model defaults may not satisfy organization-specific governance requirements without calibration/fine-tuning.
[...]
Privacy Filter does not support configuring label policies dynamically at runtime; instead changing policies requires further finetuning of the model. The native label set and associated decision boundaries may not be appropriate for every use case. For example, the model's training policy aims to prioritize personal identifiers, often preserving context that is not strongly person-linked by design; some users may want to adjust this choice.
[...]
Like all models, Privacy Filter can make mistakes, such as: under-detection of uncommon personal names, regional naming conventions, initials, honorific-heavy references, or domain-specific identifiers; over-redaction of public entities, organizations, locations, or common nouns when local context is ambiguous; fragmented or shifted span boundaries in mixed-format text, long documents, or text with heavy punctuation and layout artifacts; missed secrets for novel credential formats, project-specific token patterns, or secrets split across surrounding syntax; and over-redaction of benign high-entropy strings, placeholders, hashes, sample credentials, or synthetic examples that resemble secrets.
[...]
Additional caution is warranted in high-sensitivity settings such as medical, legal, financial, human resources, education, and government workflows. In these settings, both false negatives and false positives can be costly: missed spans may expose sensitive information, while excess masking can remove material context needed for review, auditing, or downstream decision-making.
[...]
- Use Privacy Filter as part of a holistic privacy-by-design approach, not as a blanket anonymization claim.
- Evaluate in-domain with local policy references before production.
- Use task-specific fine-tuning when policy differs from base boundaries.
- Keep human review paths for high-sensitivity workflows.

it1_edit.title: PrivRewrite: Differentially Private Text Rewriting Under Black-Box Access with Refined Sensitivity Guarantees
it1_edit.content:
Text data is indispensable for modern machine learning and natural language processing but often contains sensitive information that must be protected before sharing or release. Differential privacy (DP) provides rigorous guarantees for privacy preservation, yet applying DP to text rewriting poses unique challenges. Existing approaches frequently assume white-box access to large language models (LLMs), relying on internal signals such as logits or gradients. These assumptions limit practicality, since real-world users typically interact with LLMs only through black-box APIs. We introduce PrivRewrite, a framework for differentially private text rewriting that operates entirely under black-box access. PrivRewrite constructs a diverse pool of candidate rewrites through randomized prompting and pruning and then employs the exponential mechanism to select a single release with end-to-end ϵ -DP. A key contribution is our refined sensitivity analysis of the utility function, which yields tighter bounds than naive estimates and thereby strengthens the accuracy guarantees of the exponential mechanism. The framework requires no fine-tuning, internal model access, or local inference, making it lightweight and deployable in practical API-based settings. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PrivRewrite achieves strong privacy–utility trade-offs, producing fluent and semantically faithful outputs while upholding formal privacy guarantees. These results highlight the feasibility of black-box DP text rewriting and show how refined sensitivity analysis can further improve utility under strict privacy constraints.
[...]
Thus, in this paper, we propose PrivRewrite, a text rewriting framework that provides formal DP guarantees using only black-box access to LLMs. The method requires no internal model access, fine-tuning, or local inference, making it lightweight and practical for real-world deployment. PrivRewrite consists of two key components: (i) sanitized candidate generation via an LLM and (ii) a DP selection mechanism applied to the candidate outputs. This design achieves end-to-end ϵ -DP while preserving semantic fidelity and fluency, even in scenarios where only API-based LLM access is available.

statement: Congress prohibits the NIH from researching the cause of mass shootings.
label: false
speaker: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
true_statement: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is wrong about a ban on NIH research about mass shootings
what: prohibits the NIH from researching the cause of mass shootings
subject: Government and Political Entities
prompt: Why Congress prohibits the NIH from researching the cause of mass shootings?
answer:
Congress does **not** prohibit the National Institutes of Health (NIH) from researching the causes of mass shootings.  
The claim that “Congress prohibits the NIH from investigating mass shootings” is a misunderstanding of the *Dickey Amendment* and its subsequent clarifications.

### What the Dickey Amendment actually says
- In 1996, Congress added language to the federal appropriations bill that read:  
  > “None of the funds made available for injury prevention and control at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention may be used to advocate or promote gun control.”  
  This was originally directed at the CDC, but later extended to the NIH in 2011.  
- The amendment does **not** ban research on gun violence; it only bars the use of federal funds for *advocacy* or *promotion* of gun‑control policies.  
- Because the language was vague and politically charged, federal agencies – especially the CDC – interpreted it as a chilling prohibition and largely stopped funding gun‑violence research for more than two decades.

### Congressional clarification
- In March 2018, Congress included a statement in the omnibus spending bill that clarified the amendment’s meaning: the Department of Health and Human Services – and thus the NIH – may conduct research on the causes of gun violence, provided the research does not advocate for specific gun‑control legislation.  
- The clarification was reiterated by the HHS Secretary, who said the CDC (and by extension the NIH) has the authority to study gun‑related violence without fear of violating the amendment.  
- Since fiscal year 2020, the NIH (along with the CDC, the Office of Justice Programs, and other agencies) has awarded **millions of dollars** in grants to study firearm violence, including studies of mass shootings.  

### Current status
- The NIH is actively funding gun‑violence research; the agency has awarded grants on the causes and prevention of mass shootings.  
- No current law or congressional mandate bars the NIH from investigating mass shootings.

**Sources**  
- [PolitiFact – Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is wrong about a ban on NIH research on mass shootings](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/apr/23/robert-f-kennedy-jr/robert-f-kennedy-jr-is-wrong-about-a-ban-on-nih-re/)  
- [NCBI PMC – The Dickey Amendment on Federal Funding for Research on Gun Violence](https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5993413/)  
- [APA – “A thaw in the freeze on federal funding for gun violence and injury prevention research”](https://www.apa.org/monitor/2021/04/news-funding-gun-research)

statement: Adolf Heusinger was Adolf Hitler’s chief of staff and after World War II ended became the chief of staff for NATO forces.

prompt: Why Adolf Heusinger was Adolf Hitler’s chief of staff and after World War II ended became the chief of staff for NATO forces?
answer:
Adolf Heusinger was **not** Adolf Hitler’s chief of staff, nor did he become a chief of staff for NATO after the war.

**During World II**

* Heusinger was a senior operations officer on the German General Staff.  From 1938‑1944 he led the Operations Division of the Army’s General Staff (OKH) and was promoted to lieutenant general in 1943.  
* When General Kurt Zeitzler temporarily resigned in July 1944, Heusinger acted as chief of the Army General Staff for a short period (about two weeks) and was present in the Wolf’s Lair during the July 20 plot.  That brief assignment does **not** equate to the permanent position of “chief of staff” of the Wehrmacht or of Hitler’s overall command 【Snopes.com】【Wiki】.

**After World II**

* Heusinger was taken prisoner by the Allies in May 1945 and later cleared of war‑crimes charges.  
* He entered the post‑war German military (Bundeswehr) and in 1957 was promoted to full general and appointed **Inspector General of the West German Armed Forces** (the office equivalent to the commander‑in‑chief of the army).  He served in that role until 1961 【Wiki】.  
* In April 1961 he was appointed **Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee**, the senior military advisory body of the alliance.  He served in that position until 1964 【Wiki】.

Thus:

| Period | Position Held | Notes |
|--------|---------------|-------|
| 1940‑1944 | Operations Chief (OKH) | Senior staff officer, never the overall chief of staff. |
| Jul‑1944 | Acting Chief of Army General Staff (OKH) | Temporary, two‑week tenure. |
| 1957‑1961 | Inspector General of the West German Armed Forces | Highest-ranked German army officer. |
| 1961‑1964 | Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee | Senior NATO advisory role, **not** the “chief of staff.” |

The claim that Heusinger was Hitler’s chief of staff and then NATO’s chief of staff is therefore incorrect. His wartime role was a senior staff position, and his postwar roles were high‑ranking but distinct from a chief‑of‑staff position.
